plan: [Derive symmetric Bayes–Nash equilibrium for 5 bidders in a 3rd-price auction. Assume monotone linear bids b(v)=c·v. Maximizing expected payoff when a type v bids z and using F(z)=(z/49) gives a first-order condition that yields c=2. Thus equilibrium b(v)=2v. With independent uniform draws and no history, this maximizes long-run expected profit for each bidder. ]

[I have value $31. With 4 opponents and no history, assume they bid their values. If I bid x I win with prob (x/49)^4 and, conditional on winning, the expected third-highest opponent value is 0.6x. Expected profit = (x/49)^4*(31−0.6x). Maximizing yields x=124/3≈41.33. Given 0.1 increments, bid $41.3 to maximize my expected payoff under this reasonable model.]

[Compute symmetric equilibrium for a 3rd-price auction with 5 bidders and uniform values. Solving the first-order condition (assuming increasing bidding rule) yields a linear equilibrium bid β(v) = (4/3)v. With my value $20, the equilibrium bid is (4/3)*20 = $26.666..., rounded to the nearest $0.1.]

[ Reason: In a third-price auction with 5 bidders, if I bid high enough to win, I'll pay the second-highest of the four others. Assuming other bids follow values uniformly, the expected second-highest of 4 draws is 3/5*49 ≈ $29.4, giving expected surplus ≈ $17.6. The risk of paying above my value is negligible. So I will bid the maximum $49 to secure the win and maximize expected profit. ]

[My value is $7. In a 3rd-price auction with 5 bidders the expected 3rd-highest valuation ≈ 24.5, far above 7, so winning typically yields a loss. The probability the 3rd-highest is below 7 is only ≈2.3%, so aggressive bidding risks negative payoff. To maximize long-run profit, avoid winning this round: bid the minimum to stay out of the winner’s circle.]
